rss_7_1793138291.title: How to keep tabs on the tools in your lab
rss_7_1793138291.text:
When Greg Bannard started her master’s degree in chemistry at the University of Calgary, Canada, she didn’t have an arsenal of tools available to her, so it became incredibly frustrating when equipment went missing. And, being the sort of scientist who’s picky about the kind of spatula that she uses, it could be extremely annoying when her favourite ones disappeared. After several instances of vanishing kit, she could no longer endure running around trying to find tools that had been misplaced.

This inspired her to create a portable pouch that fitted into her pocket of her laboratory coat. “It’s mostly things that I ended up finding myself reaching for,” says Bannard, who now works as an industrial designer, but still keeps the pouch as a keepsake of her time in research.

At the time, Bannard worked in a dye lab, studying the functionality of perylene diimide dyes for the active layers of solar cells. She packed a whole lot into the pouch: a diamond glass cutter, a carbide glass cutter, an ear curette used for working with tiny amounts of powdered dye, a test-tube holder, a pencil, a spatula, little scissors, a felt marker and an “army” of tweezers. “It was a busy lab and people needed to get their own work done,” she says. “The best way that I could get my work done was knowing where everything was.”

Public-speaking tips from the experts: what scientists can learn from comics, musicians and actors

Beyond Bannard’s frustration, missing equipment can disrupt crucial scientific research. Scientists often need particular tools to keep delicate experiments on track. Momoko Takahashi, a neurobiologist at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, knows this too well. She recalls panicking when she could not find a syringe during a time-sensitive procedure involving mouse neurons. “There’s an entire domino effect that starts if one particular moment fails,” she says. “If [the experiment] is not successful, I just wasted a bunch of animals’ lives and that makes me feel really guilty.”

Everyday acts of borrowing, accidental theft, mislabelling and sample moving can turn shared laboratories into crime scenes. The social-media platform Reddit is awash with scientists asking how to guard against ‘disappearing’ items and seeking solutions to track down their missing solutions. Nature spoke directly to researchers about how they protect their work, equipment and sanity without becoming the lab secret police. After all, much ‘stealing’ is done by accident or at least not with malicious intent.

Prevent it

Put systems in place. Scientists who spoke to Nature recounted that all kinds of equipment can disappear from the lab, from small items such as pens and pipettes, to larger and more expensive equipment such as centrifuges and computers. Many interviewees emphasized the importance of having systems in place, such as inventory lists, sign-out sheets and shared equipment guidelines, so that it’s much harder for things to vanish without a trace.

Takahashi highlights the importance of centralizing organization by having official, or unofficial, lab managers and having documentation to keep track of equipment. “A lab is a small business and it should be run like a small business,” she says, noting that she has fallen into a “pseudo lab-manager” position in every lab she’s been in. “Having organizational management implemented right off the bat is crucial to making sure that everything runs smoothly.”

Sandra Petrus-Reurer, a cell-therapy researcher at the University of Cambridge, UK, also stresses the importance of having a really good inventory from the start so people can track who has used specific samples. This way, if something goes missing, it’s easier to work out when and how it could have happened.

Have clear procedures and usage rules. Procedure is especially important when several researchers share equipment or space. According to a PhD student in Australia, who wishes to remain anonymous, shared fridge and freezer space, reagents and fume hoods cause the most conflict in her facilities. To reduce issues in these communal lab spaces, the university has a booking system for benches and hoods. Everyone has allocated trays in each fridge and freezer, each with its own managed inventory to keep track of items and sample movements.

Six tips for better spreadsheets

Some expensive machines or equipment might be funded by several labs, which can also create confusion and conflict, says George Chen, a neurologist at the Children’s Hospital Los Angeles, California. Displaying who can use the equipment can make a world of difference: something as simple as a poster that explains which materials are co-owned and can be shared between labs could be enough. “Be transparent and find systems in which it’s just immediately obvious to everyone what's going on,” he says.

Mark your territory. Making ownership unmistakable can help to mitigate issues. One of the first things Takahashi did when joining her current lab was to label everything. “I always tell the undergrads to initial it or write your name on it,” she says. In Bannard’s lab, each member had electrical tape of a specific colour, which they would wrap around their designated tools. Bannard’s, for instance, was green.

The Australian PhD student says that having clearly labelled reagents and pipettes helps to provide clarity about what some people can and cannot use. After being accused of nabbing another lab’s antibodies, her lab started putting custom stickers on anything that was their property. Indeed, labelling something with a name only the lab group can understand can also ward off sticky fingers. “My lab group once made up code names for our cell lines, as previously our cell cultures were going missing,” she said. The thinking was that potential ‘thieves’ would not know what the code names corresponded to. She says that her group’s cells stopped disappearing after they started adding code names.

You might also consider using hidden labels. A former neuroscientist at the University of Oxford, UK, who preferred not to be named so as not to reveal his lab’s method, had his own hack: “We would put some marker hidden on the inside of the hardware,” he said. “Labels can easily be removed or rubbed off if they’re visible, so by using hidden labels, we could prove that misplaced equipment was ours.”

Hidden and kept under lock and key. Takahashi recommends keeping equipment in cabinets or drawers rather than leaving it out in the open where it can easily be taken or picked up by mistake. People are less likely to rifle through drawers than they are to take things from the bench, she says, noting that she used to hide her prized forceps in her drawer before she went home.

And if you need an extra level of protection, the PhD student recommends getting a lockable box or container that only you, or your team, can access. Petrus-Reurer once bought a lockable fridge, both for extra space and for the appearance of limited access: “I never removed the key, but adding a bit of a physical barrier helped.”

Minimize it

Store separately. When equipment does go missing, there are ways to lessen the impact. Petrus-Reurer and Chen recommend keeping a second stock of everything, because commonly used items tend to run out faster than scientists can replenish them and if they get stolen or misplaced, it can further this nuisance. Chen personally keeps a secondary stash of tissue-culture plates and pipette tips in a hidden drawer. “They’re not expensive, but they just seem to always disappear from the cabinets before someone can reorder them.”

Bring your own tools. Despite best efforts, tools kept communally in the lab can still go missing. “In a well-stocked lab, stuff still happens,” says Bannard. You can plan accordingly, however. Like Bannard, Chen keeps some of his own personal instruments separate, making it clear that they belong to him so that others do not accidentally — or purposefully — nab them.

rss_8_1793138293.title: Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks
rss_8_1793138293.text:
The future of psychedelics is looking bright, after some dark times. Just two years ago, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) rejected an application to use MDMA — the active ingredient in the party drug ecstasy — to treat post-traumatic stress disorder. With that refusal, the whole field seemed to stall. But now, billion-dollar investments and more clinical-trial data suggest that the field is forging ahead.

The FDA refusal “stimulated a lot of thought and conversation”, says Rachel Yehuda, a neuroscientist at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. “But it didn’t make people want to give up on these medicines. Everyone can see that loud and clear.”

In July, the drug giant Eli Lilly in Indianapolis, Indiana, announced plans to acquire AtaiBeckley, a psychedelic-medicine development firm in New York City, for up to US$3.8 billion. The company’s lead asset, BPL-003, targets treatment-resistant depression, a condition affecting millions of people around the world.

Eli Lilly’s bet is one of the largest so far. And it comes on the heels of other big investments, such as Illinois-based AbbVie’s $1.2 billion acquisition in 2025 of bretisilocin, a short-acting psychedelic being developed by Gilgamesh Pharmaceutical in New York City.

Why such persistence in the pursuit of psychedelic therapies? Researchers partially credit increasingly clear guidance from regulators worldwide on how these treatments should be studied and used. Even in the United States, where regulatory teams in the FDA have been thinned by layoffs, psychedelics are still a priority. “Where there’s a governmental will, there’s a governmental way,” says Yehuda.

Many psychedelic-development programmes have now advanced to late stages. Findings include rapid and potentially lasting effects for anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Definium Therapeutics, based in New York City, released results in August and September from late-stage studies of its LSD-based pill, showing a significant reduction in symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder. Preliminary trials also hint at psychedelic benefits for conditions such as substance-use and eating disorders.

Meanwhile, researchers are zeroing in on specific properties of psychedelics, with the goal of engineering drugs that act for less time and with fewer hallucinations — tweaks that could make them more viable in the clinic.

Magic-mushroom compound blocks a severe side effect of chemotherapy, in mice

Still, scientists emphasize that there’s much more to be done. Further research is needed to understand, for example, the extent of possible mental and physical adverse effects and how long effects of various compounds need to last to have a therapeutic benefit.

Continued progress is not inevitable. The enthusiasm seen in the late 1990s and early 2000s, which led to the increased pace of discoveries, also happened in the 1950s and 1960s. However, it was stifled by the US government-led war on drugs, says Philippe Lucas, director of research at the non-profit organization Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies in San Jose, California. “So I always have that red flag in the back of my mind.”

Still, given the big recent investments, he says, the field “looks to have significant legs”.

Boom over bust?

The failed FDA approval of MDMA initially seemed to have “a really sobering effect on the field”, says Ekaterina Malievskaia, co-founder and chief executive of n1 bio, an autism biotechnology firm in Miami, Florida, and co-founder of Compass Pathways, a psychedelic-development company headquartered in London that is trying to earn US approval of a psilocybin treatment.

In 2024, the FDA voiced specific concerns about the MDMA therapy from Lykos Therapeutics, now Resilient Pharmaceuticals in Lake Forest, Illinois. One major issue was that participants and researchers could guess whether someone was on an active psychedelic treatment during the trials, a phenomenon known as functional unblinding. This July, the FDA finalized psychedelic-trial guidance that includes advice for reducing functional unblinding.

A treatment room for psychedelics at Compass Pathways, a pharmaceutical-research company in London.Credit: Tom Jamieson/New York Times/Redux/eyevine

The agency also flagged the difficulty in disentangling MDMA’s effects from those of the accompanying psychotherapy during the trials. Both safety and efficacy probably depend on the therapeutic context, says Yehuda.

Lykos’s studies were “guinea pigs” for the industry, says Emma Wille, an analyst at business-intelligence provider Citeline in New York City. “Now, companies know more about what will make a good data-submission package.”

And many are moving forwards with applications. Resilient resubmitted a new-drug application this year. Meanwhile, Compass Pathways has announced positive results from two late-stage trials of a psilocybin therapy for treatment-resistant depression. “It does look as though it’s inevitable that they will get the license”, says Robin Carhart-Harris, a neuroscientist and psychopharmacologist at the University of California, San Francisco.

The US government seems to anticipate movement on psychedelics. An August report from the US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration in Rockville, Maryland, urges states to prepare for possible FDA approval of psychedelic therapies by, among other recommendations, building the necessary health-system infrastructure to deliver such treatments.

How ecstasy and psilocybin are shaking up psychiatry

Although MDMA and psilocybin are likely to be the first psychedelics to be “pharmaceuticalized”, says Lucas, “dark horses are running in the same room”. Among the compounds getting attention as potential therapies are 5-MeO-DMT, the primary component of the poison excreted by the Sonoran Desert toad (Incilius alvarius), which can cause an almost complete dissolution of the sense of self, and ibogaine, which has psychedelic effects that can last for more than 24 hours and carries cardiovascular risks. “Ten years ago, many of us would have thought these would be the least likely to go through pharmaceutical development,” says Lucas.

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order in April that streamlines research into psychedelic compounds and increases the government’s financial investments. The order specifically highlights ibogaine. The chemical, found in a Central African shrub, is being studied as a treatment for substance-use disorders and PTSD. In October, the FDA announced a request for public input on the design of government-funded clinical trials of ibogaine.

Odette Hauke, a regulatory-affairs consultant based in Los Angeles, California, welcomed the move. There are many unresolved safety questions, she says. “It’s important that we’re approaching this cautiously.”

FDA rejects ecstasy as a therapy: what’s next for psychedelics?

Meanwhile, scientific discoveries and technological tools are making it possible to lessen some of the ‘weirdness’ and risks of specific psychedelics. By tweaking molecules to shorten or remove the psychedelic experience, developers aim to reduce the time, supervision and cost required for treatment.

rss_9_1793138294.title: Could measuring immune health reshape medical care?
rss_9_1793138294.text:
The immune system is central to human health. When it fails, people can become more susceptible to infection and cancer. When misdirected, it can attack the body’s own tissues. And as it ages, it can contribute to chronic disease.

People of the same age can have strikingly distinct immune systems, shaped by genetics and by environmental and lifestyle factors, including air pollution, smoking, diet and past infections1,2. Growing evidence suggests that variation in the immune system’s ‘biological age’ — the rate at which it has aged, which is distinct from chronological age — matters for health. This variation has been linked to neurodegeneration, cancer and mortality risk3.

Immune cells have a surprising role in exercise endurance

Yet, clinicians have no routine way of measuring how healthy someone’s immune system is. That’s because the immune system is a dynamic network that can change over time. It involves specialized organs that support immune-cell development and function, as well as immune cells that can circulate throughout the body and reside in tissues4. Signalling molecules, such as cytokines and chemokines, allow these immune cells and tissues to communicate.

Clinical tests provide only a fragmented picture of the immune system. A physician might examine an individual’s white blood cell count to establish whether circulating immune cells are at unusually high or low levels. They might also measure blood biomarkers such as C-reactive protein, which can indicate inflammation. But neither measurement is specific to a particular health condition, and they do not indicate whether the immune system as a whole is resilient or in decline, or if it is capable of mounting an effective response to infections and other challenges.

But advances in immunology, molecular profiling, medical imaging and artificial intelligence are opening up fresh possibilities for measuring the state of people’s immune systems. The stage is set for researchers to develop the immunome: a comprehensive characterization of immune health across cells, tissues, organs and molecular interactions (see ‘Defining the immunome’).

Defining the immunome A raft of assays can provide information about the state of a person’s immune system. Potential component of an immunome Information gleaned Large-scale analysis of circulating proteins and antibodies Patterns of immune signalling and antibody recognition beyond individual clinical markers Detailed profiling of individual cells Types, abundance and molecular states of immune cells Immune-receptor sequencing Diversity and composition of immune-cell populations Detection of quantifiable features from medical images of immune-related organs Structural and compositional features of the thymus, spleen and bone marrow Spatial profiling of tissues Locations of immune cells and how they are organized relative to other cells Measurements of immune-system activity before and after immune challenges Strength, timing and persistence of responses to challenges such as vaccination Long-term modelling of immune health using artificial intelligence Several types of data can be combined to predict how ageing and disease change a person’s immune health

Research initiatives such as the Human Immunome Project, which one of us (J.S.T.) co-leads, are beginning to provide the data needed. What remains unclear is whether this information could be used to improve patient care, and how that could be achieved. Which measurements best capture clinically important aspects of a person’s immune health? How stable are these variables over time? And, most importantly, can assessing them improve clinical decision-making and, ultimately, disease outcomes?

Measuring every aspect of the immune system will not be feasible for every person. Instead, researchers should try to identify key features that can be readily assessed in the clinic to flag aspects of the immune system that are weakened, or declining quickly when they shouldn’t be. Such assessments could open avenues for disease prevention, treatment guidance and methods to monitor interventions.

For instance, these features might enable physicians to recognize cases of accelerated immune ageing and spot individuals who need close disease monitoring. For cancer treatment, measures of immune health could help to identify people who are most likely to benefit from therapies that rely on the immune system5,6, as well as those with a high risk of adverse reactions.

Such measurements could also help researchers to understand why people of similar ages and apparently similar health sometimes have substantially different responses to the same infection — a phenomenon that was apparent during the COVID-19 pandemic. Antibody responses to the same vaccine likewise vary widely between individuals2,7. If this variability could be measured, clinicians could use it to tailor preventive measures, treatments and monitoring to an individual’s immune system.

Researchers, health-care systems and funders must work to find the smallest, most scalable set of measurements that can capture meaningful differences in immune function and guide clinical decisions. Here, we outline a road map for moving the immunome from the laboratory to the clinic.

Deep research

First, scientists should generate longitudinal data sets using large research populations and biobanks. Gaining a full understanding of immune health will require measuring several components of the immune system alongside broader indicators of health and disease in the same people over time.

Analysis of genes and gene expression in single cells from large research populations and biobanks could help researchers to understand which immune-cell groups are present in distinct populations. This could reveal which genes and signalling pathways are active in particular populations of cells, and what combination of markers best distinguishes between healthy, declining and dysfunctional immune states2,3,8. Analysing blood proteins can indicate whether a person is experiencing inflammation and whether their immune system has been activated. And studying the receptors on immune cells called lymphocytes can reveal the diversity of cells available to recognize threats. These receptors determine which pathogenic antigens the cells will identify; greater diversity generally allows the immune system to detect a broader range of threats.

The Moderna cancer vaccine offers hope — now we must speed up personalized therapies

Researchers must also study how the immune system changes over time to respond to challenges. Studying people before and after they are vaccinated is one standardized way to do this. It’s already clear that a person’s immune state before vaccination can predict the strength and characteristics of the immune response that follows2,9. The task now is to find out whether a person’s response to routine vaccination could provide a practical read-out of their immune competence10, and whether it would be possible to modify the immune health of an individual before interventions such as vaccination or cancer immunotherapy to improve their response2,5.

Data sets used to probe the immunome must represent the diversity of human immunity, because genetics and environmental factors alter immune states1. For example, malaria vaccine efficacy can differ markedly between populations across continents7,11. Yet, many existing immune-profiling data sets are concentrated in populations from high-income nations. When studying diverse populations, researchers around the world should use the same protocols so that results from various regions can be compared.

A big challenge will be making sense of complex data sets. AI tools can identify patterns across thousands of immune measurements, but those patterns might reflect differences between populations, laboratories or technologies rather than underlying immune health. Models will therefore need to be tested across independent populations and over time to establish which signals are robust and clinically meaningful.

Scientists working on the Human Immunome Project are developing and applying AI approaches to immunome data collected from various populations. An important goal for the project is to create reference maps and foundation models that scientists can use for tasks such as identifying small, manageable sets of measurements that would be useful in clinical settings.

Find what works

With large-scale data in hand, researchers should work towards simplification. The success of the field should be judged not by how many immune variables can be measured, but by whether it is possible to improve clinical decision-making with just a small, manageable set of them. Tests used in the clinic would ideally be cheap and should not put extra demands on patients. Before any AI tools can be used routinely, they will need to be tested across a range of hospitals and populations. Researchers must establish whether a tool’s outputs truly improve treatment decisions.

One example of a tool that might be useful in the clinic is an AI model capable of extracting information about immune health from routine blood tests and clinical information such as age, sex, body weight and medical history. In a study published last year6, such an approach was able to predict health outcomes after immunotherapy treatment for people with cancer.

rss_10_1793138295.title: Mysterious flickering brain signals could help to unlock secrets of consciousnes
rss_10_1793138295.text:
Monkey see: macaques’ brains strongly encode visual stimuli that are outside the animals’ awareness.Credit: Pete Oxford/Nature Picture Library

The reaction to neuroscientist Doris Tsao’s latest preprint, she says, has been “surreal”. Tsao, at the University of California, Berkeley, described the study on social media on 17 October. Ten days later, her summary has drawn more than two million views and 11,000 likes.

Posted on bioRxiv, the study1 probed the brains of macaques (Macaca mulatta) during a visual-perception experiment. Using only the monkeys’ neural activity, Tsao’s team managed to reconstruct with high fidelity not only images that the animals were consciously seeing, but also images that were in front of their eyes but escaped their awareness.

Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be

Previous studies in monkeys have detected neural activity in response to content they are not aware of, but only as weak signals. “It’s super surprising to find this strong signal that is not consciously perceived,” Tsao says. Even more unexpected to Tsao, the study showed that brain activity switched between patterns associated with conscious processing and those associated with unconscious processing several times per second.

The authors say that the findings, which have not yet been peer reviewed, could be a small step towards solving one of neuroscience’s biggest mysteries: how brains give rise to consciousness, or the subjective experience of being aware.

Scientists studying consciousness were intrigued by the research and praised its rigorous methods. But some pointed out that the social-media buzz might have been overblown. “It’s an interesting little firestorm of a paper,” says John Sakon, a cognitive neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles. “But some of the findings were not totally unexpected.”

Out of sight, out of mind?

Imagine someone looking through binoculars that show a different image to each eye. The person would perceive only one image at a time, rather than a mix of the two. This phenomenon, known as binocular rivalry, is important for the study of consciousness, because it enables researchers to study what happens in the brain when an image enters someone’s consciousness.

How does the brain control consciousness? This deep-brain structure

Exploring this paradigm with monkeys, Tsao and her team presented one image of a face to one eye of a monkey and, after a couple of seconds, introduced an image of a different face to the other eye. When this experiment is done in humans, people who are shown both images report seeing only the second. Researchers assume that the same thing happens with monkeys.

The scientists recorded activity in two brain regions that are known to be involved in facial recognition: the inferotemporal cortex and the prefrontal cortex.

Researchers first showed both faces to the monkey, one at a time, so that they could identify the distinct patterns of neural activity elicited by each image. Then they began the experiment by introducing the first image to one eye. When they introduced the second image to the monkey’s other eye, its brain activity quickly flickered between two neural patterns 15 times per second.

rss_11_1793138297.title: Global climate body fights for survival: why the IPCC must be saved
rss_11_1793138297.text:
The UN organization faces perhaps the most serious crisis in its nearly 40-year history — but it is too precious to lose.

The IPCC has survived crises before — it can do so again.Credit: Pavlo Gonchar/SOPA Images/Sipa USA/Alamy

When the most recent meeting of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), held in Addis Ababa, ended earlier this month, its conclusion drew negative media headlines. The United Nations body — the world’s forum for climate scientists — had failed, not for the first time, to agree a timetable for its next comprehensive review of the science of global climate change.

Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming

Many countries would like the review, known as the Seventh Assessment Report (AR7), to be published in 2028. This would be in time for a UN climate meeting called the Global Stocktake, at which countries assess their progress towards meeting climate pledges. A number of nations, including some European countries and small island states, want the report to be published ahead of the stocktake. This would allow decisions such as adjustments to pledges to be informed by the latest science.

A second, smaller group, including India, Iran, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia, is arguing that 2028 is too soon. They say that some of the poorest countries lack the capacity to participate in the process of reviewing the report before it is published. They also object to the fact that the studies under review are dominated by science from institutions in high-income countries. However, for AR7, the IPCC says 51% of authors and review editors are from developing countries and nations with economies in transition.

Reviewing IPCC assessment reports is a big undertaking. When AR6 was published in 2023, it ran to more than 7,500 pages and received some 200,000 comments from reviewers around the world.

But the IPCC faces an even more serious problem: it is running out of money. For the first time in its history, it might not have the funds to finish an assessment report. The body relies on voluntary donations from governments and other UN agencies, and these have been falling since 2023 (see ‘Lack of trust’). The funds are also used to support scientists from the poorest countries, allowing them to attend meetings. Many of the countries that want to delay the next report have contributed nothing to the IPCC in years, if ever, although Russia is a notable exception. If contributions continue at current levels, by the end of 2028 the IPCC will be left with just 5 million Swiss francs (US$6 million) — the amount needed for an orderly wind-down of the body.

Source: IPCC

But there is a way forwards. The IPCC needs more than 20 million Swiss francs to stay operational until the end of 2029, and to complete AR7. Nations must consider increasing their contributions immediately. Other donors, including philanthropists and non-governmental organizations, should also approach the IPCC to see how they can help.

There are those who question whether the world still needs the IPCC. They say that there are faster ways to synthesize climate research, and that much is already known about climate change, its impacts and the measures needed to prevent dangerous consequences. Last week, a separate UN report confirmed that countries are not on track to limit global warming to within 1.5 °C of pre-industrial levels.

How to fight climate change without the US: a guide to global action

But these arguments overlook the true value of the IPCC, which includes its processes. IPCC reports are produced in a highly consultative way — scientists from the richest to the poorest countries collaborate, ensuring that voices from around the world are heard. This global, scientist-led process also ensures that the quality of the evidence under review takes precedence over political considerations. Once the scientists agree on the main text, governments are involved in writing the summary report, and can choose whether and how to act on the findings. But they cannot change the main text of the assessment report.

The IPCC has survived crises before. One of the most serious was in 1995, when AR2 concluded that “the balance of the evidence” suggested humans are responsible for global warming. This was challenged by representatives of some fossil-fuel-producing countries and oil and gas companies. But the organization’s scientists stood firm, often at great personal cost. Most IPCC-sponsoring governments backed the scientists, and the crisis eventually passed.

The current crisis is more serious because it concerns the IPCC’s very survival. Ideally, governments would come together again and ensure that the organization is properly funded. One way to resolve the matter would be to replace the current process of ad hoc voluntary contributions with multi-year budgetary commitments, similarly to those used to fund many other UN agencies. Support from non-governmental sources should also be considered.

The timing of the next assessment report must be resolved. But the dispute must not be allowed to distract from the most important matter of all: ensuring the continued survival of the IPCC itself.

rss_12_1793138298.title: Can scientists reliably tell if a novel is written using AI?
rss_12_1793138298.text:
Tuhin Chakrabarty is a computer scientist at the State University of New York at Stony Brook who studies how to detect AI-generated text. His research drew global attention earlier this year after a journalist cited it as supporting evidence to claim that significant portions of the bestselling 2026 novel Daggermouth were produced using artificial intelligence — an allegation that the book’s author, H. M. Wolfe, has denied. Nature spoke to Chakrabarty about his work, why it matters and what the rise of AI means for the future of creativity.

How did you become interested in detecting AI-generated writing?

I live in New York City, and I’m surrounded by creative people. I can understand why artists are enraged about AI. It can take years to write a book, but an AI chatbot can churn one out in 15 minutes. That got me interested in the subject of copyright and creativity. As AI use spreads, the future is going to get messier. What qualifies for copyright protection? How do you quantify the original human contribution when something is co-created with AI? How can you even tell the two apart?

What should count as AI-written text?

Disclosure is important. At scientific conferences, we are seeing increasing numbers of disclosures stating that AI was used and for what — to polish writing, say, or for copy-editing. Once you disclose, things become easier to judge.

Can Anthropic’s invisible watermarks curb ‘AI slop’? Researchers remain sceptical

Over time, you could imagine separate markets developing for text written purely by people, hybrid writing and mass-market AI-written prose. That might create better economic incentives for people who don’t use AI or are morally opposed to its use. Everyone’s process is different, and there is a huge spectrum in how AI can be used. My moral concern relates to people who use AI, but pass off AI-written prose as their own. That is where the problem lies.

How can AI-written prose be detected?

In a July preprint, my colleagues and I traced relatively unusual sequences of words that appear verbatim in different books (T. Chakrabarty et al. Preprint at arXiv https://doi.org/rsp2; 2026). We wanted to measure how much language books derive from books that came before them.

We compared the number of these rare expressions across three types of book for sale on Amazon. We looked at 200 titles flagged by the AI-detection software Pangram as containing substantial amounts of AI-written text, 200 self-published bestsellers with no AI-written text, and 200 literary fiction books that had won or been nominated for prizes. In each case, we identified rare expressions that appeared, word-for-word, in a sample of hundreds of thousands of titles on Google Books.

We found that literary fiction contained the least overlap with existing books, writing by self-published authors contained more and the AI-written books contained the most.

This suggests that AI models will find it easiest to automate more formulaic writing. A lot of self-published genre fiction uses tropes, clichés and formulae. These are relatively easy for AI to produce. Literary fiction requires a lot of originality and subtext. In work in progress, we divided books into narrative beats — the individual events or plot points that make up a story. There, too, we found that AI-generated books copy specific beats from earlier books written by people.

Why does AI-written text use words or expressions from existing books?

Large language models are trained on enormous amounts of human writing, including books, and sometimes specific sequences of language resurface in what they generate. We also find AI-written books containing expressions that occur in other AI-authored books. It isn’t necessarily that the model is deliberately copying a sentence from a particular book. Its output is a function of the material it was trained on, and sometimes that produces these unusually specific overlaps.

Couldn’t human writers repeat expressions from the published record, as well?

Absolutely. Two writers could reasonably produce an overlap of five or six words independently, particularly in genre fiction, because of the way it relies on formulae. But as an expression gets longer and more specific, it becomes harder to explain through coincidence. Many of the expressions we found in genre fiction were imagery, metaphors, clichés and hackneyed language. I can see why it is easier for AI to borrow those things, because if you’re writing romance or science fiction, you are also conforming to genre norms.

Your work has been used to make claims about particular books. How do you feel about that?

In our study, we chose not to name authors. As academics, we have little power. If someone brought a defamation suit against me or the university where I work, as a pre-tenured faculty member, that would be difficult to deal with.

But when a journalist is writing about your work, especially something as explosive as this, you have to share the underlying data. I shared them with The Atlantic. I was comfortable with that because I could stand by my results, and I trusted the reporter to do his due diligence.

The author of Daggermouth emphatically denies using AI. Why do you stand by your analysis?

The book contained specific rare expressions. One was: “They collapsed together, a tangle of sweat-slicked limbs and racing hearts.” That entire expression also appears in another book. It is too long and specific to occur in exactly the same way by coincidence. We found several examples like that.

Could AI help you to write your next paper?

Our checks with the AI-detection tool Pangram also flagged more than half of the book as AI-generated. I don’t think the book is 100% AI-generated, but I stand by our conclusion that it substantially used AI.

[H. M. Wolfe did not respond to a query from Nature. But, in a statement made to The Atlantic through her lawyer, she said it was “wholly untrue” that she used generative AI to write Daggermouth. Both the US publisher Simon & Schuster and the UK publisher Tor Bramble stand by the author and the book.]

Could AI also be used creatively in literature?

Absolutely. Brilliant writers have used AI. Searches (2025) by Vauhini Vara is a fascinating example of non-fiction that engages with AI-generated text. Vara uses AI responses in the book in a way that interrogates what the technology is doing. Sheila Heti also experimented with AI in her 2023 New Yorker story ‘According to Alice’. Heti conversed with a customizable chatbot on the Chai AI platform, then removed her own questions and edited the responses into the published story.

I don’t think there is necessarily a stigma about using AI. There is a stigma about using AI and hiding it. If you use AI in a profound way that adds new meaning to literature and art, why not? If an accomplished writer uses it, discloses it and produces something that wows people, I’m sure publishers will publish that.

rss_13_1793138300.title: Nerve activity initiates autoimmune hair loss
rss_13_1793138300.text:
“I’m as free as my hair,” proclaims the pop star Lady Gaga in her song ‘Hair’. Indeed, hair can be a statement of freedom and it informs our sense of self. Conversely, baldness (a condition called alopecia) can be considered an attack on the self, not only in a psychological sense, but also in a literal sense through autoimmunity, in which immune cells that usually ignore the body’s own tissues instead damage organs and cause problems such as hair loss. Writing in Nature, Cui et al.1 provide insights into autoimmune hair loss from their studies of mice.

Nature 658, 1131-1132 (2026)

rss_14_1793138301.title: Women might have invented language — but not alone
rss_14_1793138301.text:
The Revolutionary Origins of Language Chris Knight & Jerome Lewis Yale Univ. Press (2026)

The origins of writing and script remain unclear, but those of speech and language are simply unknown. This is because no physical evidence remains of the earliest language, which was probably spoken in Africa, the birthplace of Homo sapiens. By contrast, inscribed marks on clay tablets that constitute the earliest known form of writing — however mysterious — have survived from ancient Mesopotamia, dating to the fourth millennium bc.

Humanity spoke thousands of languages at the dawn of farming — now many of them are lost

That’s left a lot of room for scholars to speculate on how speech and language began, starting with thinkers from the ancient world, including Plato, who could not decide whether language had a natural or a purely human origin. By the nineteenth century, anthropologists had grown tired of so much talk with scant evidence to go on.

In 1866, the founding statutes of the Paris Linguistic Society forbade all discussion of the subject, note anthropologists Chris Knight and Jerome Lewis in The Revolutionary Origins of Language. “Anyone theorizing about the origins of language risked being dismissed as a crank.” Even so, “from time to time, this or that brave maverick would risk whatever reputation they had by attempting to reopen the debate”.

Science of linguistics

The best known, if controversial, attempts since then come from linguist Noam Chomsky, starting in the 1960s. The authors discuss his contributions at length, drawing on Knight’s book Decoding Chomsky (2016).

How the world’s largest language family spread — and why others go extinct

In 1987, Chomsky remarked in Language and Problems of Knowledge that: “There is a long history of study of the origin of language, asking how it came from the calls of apes and so forth.” But, in his view, this investigation is a “complete waste of time”.

That’s because language is based on “an entirely different principle than any animal communication system”, he wrote. Although human gestures might have evolved from animal communication systems, the same could not apply to human language, Chomsky thought.

This view was supported by an academic study, launched in 1973, of a young chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) with the punning name Nim Chimpsky. Nim learnt from his human supervisors how to make dozens of hand signs to procure food and other rewards, but not how to communicate in American Sign Language or to speak a language. “Give orange me give eat orange me eat orange give me eat orange give me you” was Nim’s longest recorded sign-language sequence, as cited by Knight and Lewis.

Nim Chimpsky the chimpanzee was taught how to make hand signs for food and other rewards.Credit: Mel Finkelstein/NY Daily News Archive/Getty

In Chomsky’s view, human language arose suddenly because of a single genetic mutation, not from Darwinian natural selection or through a gradual, adaptive cultural process. In other words, argue the authors, by declaring language to be “an especially intriguing and mysterious aspect of the natural world, to be investigated using the normal methods of natural science”, Chomsky elevated the study of linguistics to a scientific challenge in the field of anthropology.

However, they add, “there is no measuring device, magnifying glass, telescope or other instrument which can grasp the meaning of a word.” So how can conventional science investigate language?

Social origins

Rejecting Chomsky’s view, Knight and Lewis instead offer a complex mixture of evidence, both scientific and cultural, to support their own theory. This evidence is mostly drawn from prehistoric and present-day Africa, where Lewis spent three decades studying hunter-gatherers, notably the BaYaka people in Central Africa.

“To qualify as science, a hypothesis must suggest testable predictions,” the authors remark. Given that there can be no direct evidence for events in the distant past, scientists must therefore “construct tests from a wide range of telltale clues”. These include: “recurrent structures of magical myth, initiation rituals, hunters’ taboos, patterns of menstrual prohibition, lunar and solar influences, and critically, archaeological evidence for symbolism in the form of red ochre pigments and personal ornaments”. All of these clues are examined in their intriguing, if rambling, book.

AI is helping to decode animals’ speech. Will it also let us talk with them?

Although anthropologists have often suggested that speech and language arose from hunting or warfare, Knight and Lewis refute these two theories. While hunting in the forest, male hunter-gatherers “do their utmost to avoid having to speak aloud”, so as to lure animals towards them. Instead, they use sign language to alert each other to the nearby presence of animals such as gorillas, antelopes, leopards and elephants.

rss_15_1793138303.title: Daily briefing: The Selfish Gene, 50 years on
rss_15_1793138303.text:
What biologists think of Dawkins’s big idea now. Plus. how the subject of a new film haunts science and a bacterium that makes its own MOFs.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

In You Can See Everything, filmmaker Nathan Fielder (left) captured Elizabeth Holmes’s final days with her family before she went to prison for defrauding investors.Credit: A24/Everett Collection

Elizabeth Holmes and her failed blood-testing start-up, Theranos — subject of the new documentary You Can See Everything — left “a crater in the whole field of monitoring and diagnostics”, says bioengineer Paul Yager. But the field hasn’t given up on the promise of blood tests that are faster, more convenient and more accessible than current methods.

Nature | 8 min read

The newly described Infernogallus jamesi — or ‘hell chicken’ — is among the first non-bird dinosaurs thought to have exclusively eaten fruit. The species, about the size of a modern turkey, lived around 120 million years ago. Analysis of bones in an I. jamesi fossil revealed that it probably had a weak bite, strong lower-jaw muscles associated with gnashing and ridges across its beak — adaptations that closely resemble those of modern fruit-eating parrots. Researchers hypothesize that the dinosaur ate the ancient equivalent of fruits such as cherries and peaches.

Science | 5 min read

Reference: Nature Communications paper

137 The number of cancer drugs that will be made cheaper in India after a patient, Sarojam Radhakrishnan, successfully petitioned the government to lower the cost of treatment. The move imposes a maximum 30% markup on the price of these medicines — down from the current average of 170%. (The Guardian | 7 min read)

For the first time, researchers have discovered living creatures that make their own MOFs — metal-organic frameworks — with exceptional conductivity. Chemists Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry last year for their work on synthetic MOFs. Candidatus Electrothrix gigas is relatively huge — up to 8 µm long — and appears to produce centimetre-long filaments of a nickel-based MOF that help it to access energy and electron sources in the sediment of the seafloor.

Chemistry World | 7 min read (free registration required)

Reference: Nature Communications paper

Features & opinion

The idea set out in Richard Dawkins’s 1976 book The Selfish Gene — that bodies are just genes’ way of making more of themselves — “seemed pretty harmless”, writes historian of science Nathaniel Comfort. Today, “the determinism baked into the ‘gene’s-eye view’ in the book troubles me, as does the passivity of the organism in Dawkins’s telling”. Comfort dives into modern efforts to synthesize ecology, evolution, genetics and developmental biology to create “a less gene-centred view” that “is more accurate — and infinitely more satisfying”.

Nature | 11 min read

A new PhD student whose disability requires rest has found themselves in a lab where long hours are rampant, colleagues are burnt out and time off is a no-go. They ask: ‘should I risk disability stigma by disclosing to my principal investigator?’ Four researchers weigh in on how to proceed. “Regardless of what you decide about your PI, informal goodwill evaporates under pressure, while documented accommodations do not,” says management researcher Deepti Sharma.

Nature | 9 min read

As the El Niño weather event turns up the heat in oceans already warmed by climate change, scientists are turning to a suite of unorthodox methods to save temperature-sensitive corals. Underwater speakers that play the sounds of a healthy coral reef can encourage free-roaming larvae to settle in areas where adult corals are struggling, and a low-tech ‘one-star hotel’ helps to raise resilient youngsters.

Nature | 12 min video

rss_16_1793138304.title: Are salaries getting worse? Many scientists think so
rss_16_1793138304.text:
Nature’s 2026 job satisfaction survey This article is the second in a series discussing the results of Nature’s 2026 science-job satisfaction survey. It’s the latest edition of such surveys, which started in 2010; the last two took place in 2018 and 2021. The 2026 survey, created in partnership with Thinks Insight & Strategy, a research consultancy in London, launched in May and was advertised on nature.com, in Springer Nature digital products and through e-mail campaigns. It had 3,882 self-selecting respondents across 133 countries with 31% describing themselves as female and 19% as belonging to a minority ethnic group in their country of work. The full survey data sets are available at go.nature.com/4b2drrc.

Umar, a mathematics lecturer in northern Nigeria, has worked at his university for more than ten years. In that time, he’s had only one pay rise: in 2024, when the government raised the national minimum wage. With no inflation- or promotion-based adjustments, his income no longer covers his basic living costs. Instead, he has to borrow money, take on extra jobs and cut back on essential spending. “Unfortunately, my experience is not an isolated one” for Nigerian scientists, he says.

On the other side of the Atlantic Ocean, Ashley — an early-career physicist employed on a fixed-term contract in a university in the eastern United States — says she is much worse off than her parents, neither of whom have degrees. “It’s really messed up that I have a job that requires a PhD in science, yet I’m paid US$20,000 less per year than my father earned at his job 20 years ago, before accounting for inflation.” Ashley lists the things she can’t afford, including children (her pay won’t cover childcare, nor putting them through university) and home ownership. She thinks she did everything ‘right’ — for example, having jobs alongside her undergraduate studies to avoid debt. “Yet I am still locked out of the middle-class existence I have worked myself half to death for,” she says, adding: “It sucks. It really, really sucks.”

Umar and Ashley (not their real names) live in countries with vastly different resources for research and costs of living. But their stories reflect a global theme. When Nature’s careers team surveyed them and nearly 4,000 other scientists earlier this year about their salaries, less than half said they had received a pay rise in the past 12 months. Around one-third said that their salaries covered only basic expenses, and one in ten said their income failed to do even that.

The survey asked respondents to convert their gross (before-taxes) salary into US dollars, then choose the range into which it falls. More than half earn less than US$50,000 a year, and 22% make at least $80,000. In 2021, when Nature last ran this survey, 38% earned below $50,000 and 32% earned $80,000 or more. But this apparent drop in global salaries might be because of geographical shifts in those surveyed — particularly a rise in respondents from Asia, who made up 10% in 2021 and 39% this year. From continents with enough respondents for comparison, North American scientists earn the most, followed by those in Europe, then Asia (see ‘The scientist’s wallet’).

Industry salaries exceed those in academia by 66%, and more scientists in industry are satisfied with their salary (58%) than are those in academia (43%). But even in the private sector, some think that they should earn more. “It feels like I’m making less and less every year,” says a researcher working at a biomedical technology company in a large city in the midwestern United States, who, like many scientists Nature spoke to, asked to remain anonymous when discussing pay concerns.

She moved from working at a university to her current job four years ago after discovering that she was pregnant, because she judged childcare expenses to be unaffordable on her previous salary. But despite having a dozen years of work experience in both industry and academia, she says that she is still paid like a recent graduate.

“I love science and what I do, but I also feel undervalued,” she says.

Purchasing power

Scientists in the United States earn the most out of the ten countries in the survey that had more than 100 respondents, which means the results from these nations can be compared sensibly. Some 65% of United States-based scientists report earning more than $80,000 a year. The lowest wages are found in India, where 53% earn less than $15,000 a year. Comparing continents, the lowest salaries are found in Africa, where 61% earn below $15,000 per year.

We need to talk about salaries in science

However, the survey’s self-reported salary figures in converted US dollars do not reflect what those incomes can buy on the ground. A dollar buys more in India than in the United States: nearly five times more. According to purchasing-power calculations by the International Monetary Fund, a $15,000 salary in India is comparable to a $70,000 salary in the United States. When adjusted for purchasing power, average salaries in the survey for Canada overtake those in the United States, salaries in Germany come close to US ones and the wide salary gaps between emerging economies and wealthier nations shrink. And it’s important to note that a nation’s average salary in the survey can be skewed by sample biases with respect to factors such as location within a nation, employment sector and career stage.

In Brazil, where 21% of respondents report earning less than $15,000, a low or modest salary by US or western-European standards can “provide a reasonably comfortable life locally”, especially outside the most expensive cities such as Rio de Janeiro or Sao Paolo, says Haroldo Ribeiro, a physicist at the State University of Maringá in Brazil. “Still, I would not conclude that Brazilian scientists are generally well paid,” he says. Although salaries in public universities there have increased in the past few years, this comes after a long period of stagnation, he says, making it a recovery, not a raise.

Strings attached

Only 44% of people in the total sample are satisfied with their pay, but this varies between countries. Significantly more scientists in Canada (61%), Germany (68%) and the United States (55%) are satisfied with their income than the global average. The countries with at least 100 respondents that had the lowest numbers of scientists satisfied with their salary are Turkey (27%), China (39%) and Italy (40%).

China’s lower-than-average satisfaction with salary comes despite survey data suggesting that Chinese salaries have risen in US-dollar terms since Nature asked scientists the same question in 2021. Some 11% of Chinese respondents reported earning more than $80,000 this year, nearly doubling from 6% in 2021. Over the same time, in the United Kingdom, the proportion earning more than $80,000 grew from 19% to only 22%.

Salaries can vary substantially between China’s economically developed coastal areas, and its more-sparsely populated west, as well as between universities, says survey respondent Jingrui Sun, a freshwater ecologist at Yunnan University in Kunming, China. He describes his salary as “sufficient for me to live comfortably”, and says that it is common for research-intensive universities and institutions in wealthy parts of the country to offer employees performance-related pay, as well as housing subsidies and laboratory start-up packages.

But good salaries in China come with extra demands, Sun says. “Part of the package is linked to periodic assessments, and if the required targets are not met, remuneration in the following period can be reduced substantially.” He says a few of his colleagues have had their pay docked this year, after their university introduced more-stringent assessment criteria. “Such changes can have real consequences for staff retention, and have prompted academics to leave and take positions at other institutions,” he says.

Falling behind

Annual pay rises are not the global norm, the survey shows. Only 45% of respondents say they had received a raise in the previous 12 months, and 6% report a cut in pay. Industry researchers are more likely than the average result to have had a pay rise (54%), whereas the opposite is true for those who earn less than $50,000 a year (42% of whom received one).

Many survey-takers are frustrated that they aren’t getting paid more. One non-tenure-track US researcher who works in a biology department says that she exceeds her department’s tenure criteria and outperforms several of her tenure-track colleagues. Those colleagues are paid at least $20,000 more than her annually and get more research funding. “Yet my department chairs keep looking me dead in the eye and saying there’s no appetite for raises” for people like her, she says.

What’s the secret sauce for happy scientists at work? These eight countries offer some clues

When salaries grow, it’s often not enough. One researcher with a fixed-term contract in Pune, India, says his public-sector salary has not kept up with “skyrocketing urban inflation” in the city of seven million people. He says that rent, public transport and groceries consume most of his pay. “At this salary, no one can even think of home or car loans,” he says. Add a child, he says, and “it’s just a matter of survival”.

In Europe, where 27% of respondents report earning more than $80,000 a year, salaries vary massively between countries, says Norbert Bencze, president of Eurodoc, an organization for early-career researchers in Europe. “A good salary in the Netherlands is something very different from a good salary in Poland or Hungary.” However, living costs outpacing pay increases are a common problem across the continent, he says. “Some researchers have seen their actual purchasing power fall quite radically, in some cases cut in half over the past ten years, even though they got regular pay rises.” Although Nature’s salary survey was of post-PhD researchers and lab technicians, Eurodoc’s survey of doctoral pay in 2025 showed that PhD students earned below minimum wage in five European countries: Hungary, Ireland, Poland, Romania and Ukraine (see go.nature.com/4s7m1tu).

Fairer, more transparent salary-setting would be welcome, even if scientists’ wages continue to underwhelm, survey participants say. “It is not only about paying more, but about making compensation feel clear, consistent and linked to contribution,” says a materials scientist in India. People should understand how salaries are decided, what the path to a raise or promotion looks like and whether their pay is competitive with the market, he says.

Researchers who had not taken the survey felt similarly when Nature spoke to them about the results. In Portugal, academic salaries have risen in recent years, mainly to keep up with inflation, says Ronaldo Sousa, an aquatic ecologist at the Interdisciplinary Centre of Marine and Environmental Research near Porto. However, to get a pay rise that is substantially above inflation, scientists must move up the academic ladder, for example from assistant professor to associate professor. “We might publish a dozen high-impact papers in a year, but this will not necessarily result in any increase in salary,” he says.
